statement: Raffle tickets are numbered from $1$ to $500$. A ticket wins a prize if its number is divisible by $6$ but not divisible by $9$. How many tickets win a prize?

choices.misconception: I counted the 83 multiples of 6 and subtracted all 55 multiples of 9, but most multiples of 9 are not multiples of 6, so I removed too many.
I removed the multiples of $6 \cdot 9 = 54$, but the numbers divisible by both 6 and 9 are the multiples of their least common multiple, 18.
I counted all the multiples of 6 and forgot to remove the ones that are also divisible by 9.

hints: Count the multiples of 6 first, then remove some of them.
Remove the multiples of 6 that are also multiples of 9. Those are exactly the multiples of the least common multiple of 6 and 9.
There are $\lfloor 500 / 6 \rfloor = 83$ multiples of 6 and $\lfloor 500 / 18 \rfloor = 27$ multiples of 18.

solutions.reliable: Multiples of 6 up to 500: $\lfloor 500 \div 6 \rfloor = 83$, the largest being 498. A multiple of 6 is also divisible by 9 exactly when it is a multiple of $\operatorname{lcm}(6, 9) = 18$, and there are $\lfloor 500 \div 18 \rfloor = 27$ of those, the largest being 486. So $83 - 27 = 56$ tickets win. The idea: to count numbers divisible by $a$ but not by $b$, subtract the multiples of $\operatorname{lcm}(a, b)$ from the multiples of $a$.
solutions.elegant: In each run of 18 numbers, the multiples of 6 come in a group of three, and only the last of the three is a multiple of 18. The first 81 multiples of 6 form 27 such groups with $27 \cdot 2 = 54$ winners, and the last two, 492 and 498, both win: $54 + 2 = 56$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
